items.title: A hit rate's standard error
items.prose: A market-making strategy won 360 of its last 600 trades. Treat the trades as independent, each a win with chance $p$.
items.question: What is the standard error of the hit rate $\hat p = 0.6$, in %?

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{0.24/600} = 0.02$. So 60% sits five standard errors above 50%.
feedback.generic: Use $\mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$.

byKey.sd-one: You found the sd of one trade, $\sqrt{0.24} = 0.49$. Divide it by $\sqrt{600}$ for the hit rate.
byKey.no-root: You divided the variance by $n$ but took no square root. 0.0004 is a variance, not a standard error.

explain.text: One trade is a win or a loss, with variance $\hat p(1 - \hat p) = 0.24$. Averaging 600 trades divides the variance by 600. The root of 0.0004 is 0.02, or 2 percentage points.

items.title: Framing the claim
items.prose: A broker's orders have filled 62% of the time for years. After a fee change, a trader suspects fills have dropped. She will test this on next month's orders. Write $f$ for the true fill rate now.
items.question: Which pair of hypotheses fits her test?

options.why: You put her suspicion in the null. The null is the no-change position the data must argue against.

options.text: $H_0: \hat f = 0.62$ against $H_1: \hat f < 0.62$
options.why: You wrote the hypotheses about the sample rate $\hat f$. Hypotheses are about the true rate $f$.

options.text: $H_0: f = 0.58$ against $H_1: f < 0.58$, with 58% last month's rate
options.why: You centred the test on an observed rate. The null value is the long-run 62% that the claim disputes.

feedback.correct: The null is no change. The alternative is her suspected drop.
feedback.generic: The claim she wants evidence for goes in $H_1$. Both hypotheses are about the true rate $f$.

explain.text: A test asks whether the data contradict a default. Here the default is the long-run rate, $f = 0.62$. Her suspicion is a drop, so $H_1: f < 0.62$ is one-sided.

items.title: A hedge ratio
items.prose: A desk holds £2m of a stock and hedges it with index futures. In daily returns, the stock's sd is 1.5%, the index's 1.0%, and their correlation 0.8.
items.question: The hedge ratio is the slope of the stock's returns on the index's. How much of the future should the desk sell, in £m?

feedback.correct: Each 1% index move comes with 1.2% in the stock on average. So sell 1.2 times £2m.
feedback.generic: The least squares slope is $b = r\,s_y/s_x$. Multiply the position by it.

byKey.no-r: You used the ratio of the sds, 1.5. The slope also needs the correlation: $r\,s_y/s_x$.
byKey.flipped: You divided the index's sd by the stock's. That is the slope of the index on the stock.
byKey.r-only: You used the correlation alone. It has no units; the slope rescales it by $s_y/s_x$.

explain.text: The slope is $b = r\,s_y/s_x = 0.8 \times 1.5/1.0 = 1.2$. So £2m of stock moves like £2.4m of index. Selling £2.4m of futures cancels that market exposure.

items.title: Bias bought for variance
items.prose: Two estimators of a fund's true annual alpha. A, the fund's own average, is unbiased with sd 4%. B shrinks A towards zero. B's bias is $-1.5$% and its sd is 2%.
items.question: What is the mean squared error of B, in (%)²?

feedback.correct: $(-1.5)^2 + 2^2 = 6.25$, well below A's 16. A little bias bought a large cut in variance.
feedback.generic: MSE is variance plus squared bias: $E[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \mathrm{bias}^2$.

byKey.var-only: You kept only the variance, $2^2 = 4$. The MSE adds the squared bias too.
byKey.bias-only: You kept only the squared bias. B's own spread, $2^2$, counts as well.
byKey.add-first: You added the bias and the sd, then squared. The MSE adds the squares: $1.5^2 + 2^2$.
byKey.a-mse: 16 is A's MSE, $4^2$ with no bias. The question asks about B.

explain.text: For B, variance plus squared bias is $4 + 2.25 = 6.25$. A is unbiased but has MSE $4^2 = 16$. By mean squared error, the biased B is the better estimator.

items.title: A Sharpe ratio's p-value
items.prose: A strategy shows an annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.6 over 9 years of independent returns. Test $H_0$: true Sharpe 0, against $H_1$: true Sharpe above 0. You are told $\Phi(1.8) = 0.9641$.
items.question: What is the one-sided p-value? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Find $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T$ with $T$ in years. Then take the upper tail beyond $t$.

byKey.two-sided: You doubled the tail. $H_1$ points one way, so only the upper tail counts.
byKey.cdf: You gave $\Phi(1.8)$, the chance of a smaller $t$. The p-value is the tail beyond: $1 - 0.9641$.

explain.text: The Sharpe ratio's standard error is about $1/\sqrt T$, with $T$ in years. So $t = 0.6 \times 3 = 1.8$ and $p = 1 - \Phi(1.8) = 0.0359$. That clears 5% only if this was the one strategy tried.

items.title: Fit, then predict
items.prose: Five days of returns, in %.
items.question: Fit the least squares line of $y$ on $x$. What does it predict for the stock on a day the market falls 3%?

widget.label: Predicted stock return in per cent

feedback.generic: Find $b = \sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) / \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$. Then $a = \bar y - b\bar x$.

byKey.no-int: You used $\hat y = bx$ and dropped the intercept $a = 0.3$.
byKey.mean: You predicted the average day and ignored the market. The slope says the stock moves with it.
byKey.sd-ratio: You used the ratio of the sds as the slope. Least squares gives $S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 1.25$.

explain.text: $\bar x = 0$ and $\bar y = 0.3$. The cross-products sum to 12.5 and the squared $x$ deviations to 10, so $b = 1.25$. At $x = -3$, $\hat y = 0.3 - 3.75 = -3.45$.

items.title: What the 95% means
items.prose: A strategy has 400 days of returns. Its 95% confidence interval for the true mean daily return $\mu$ is 0.01% to 0.15%.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Over many repeats of the 400 days, 95% of intervals built this way would contain $\mu$.
There is a 95% chance that $\mu$ lies between 0.01% and 0.15%.
options.why: You put the chance on $\mu$. $\mu$ is fixed; the 95% belongs to the method that builds the interval.

options.text: 95% of the strategy's daily returns fall between 0.01% and 0.15%.
options.why: You read it as a range for single days. It is a range for the mean; daily returns spread far wider.

options.text: The next 400 days will average between 0.01% and 0.15% with chance 95%.
options.why: You read it as a forecast of the next average. That average has its own noise on top.

feedback.correct: The 95% is the method's long-run hit rate, not a chance about this one interval.
feedback.generic: Ask what is random. The interval is; $\mu$ is not.

explain.text: Before the data arrive, $\bar X \pm 1.96\,s/\sqrt n$ covers $\mu$ with chance 95%. Afterwards this interval either contains $\mu$ or not. It excludes 0, so the mean is positive at the 5% level.

items.title: Funding a dud
items.prose: A fund tests each new strategy against $H_0$: no edge, at 5%. One strategy with truly no edge passes, and receives £10m of capital.
items.question: Which error has the fund made?

options.text: A type I error: rejecting a true null
A type II error: failing to reject a false null
options.why: You swapped the two. A type II error misses a real edge; here a fake one got through.

options.text: No error: passing the test showed the edge is real
options.why: You took a pass as proof. A 5% test lets through about 1 in 20 strategies with no edge.

options.text: A lack of power
options.why: Power is the chance of catching a real edge. This strategy had none, so power does not apply.

feedback.correct: It rejected $H_0$ when $H_0$ was true: a false positive.
feedback.generic: Was the null true or false here, and did the test reject it?

explain.text: Rejecting a true null is a type I error; its chance per dud is $\alpha = 5\%$. Missing a real edge would be type II. Funding a dud is the costly false positive a backtest must guard against.

items.title: Alpha and beta, tested
items.prose: Ten years of a fund's monthly excess returns are regressed on the market's. The fit gives $\hat\alpha = 0.36\%$ a month, standard error 0.15%. It gives $\hat\beta = 1.15$, standard error 0.05.
items.question: Fill in the table.

feedback.correct: $t_\alpha = 2.4$ and $t_\beta = 3.0$. 0.36% a month is 4.32% a year.
feedback.generic: Each $t$ is (estimate minus null value) over its standard error. The null for beta here is 1, not 0.

explain.text: $0.36/0.15 = 2.4$, so the alpha is significant at 5% with 118 degrees of freedom. $(1.15 - 1)/0.05 = 3.0$: the fund carries more market risk than the index. A monthly mean annualises by multiplying by 12.

items.title: The rate of trades
items.prose: Gaps between trades in a quiet stock are modelled as independent exponential with rate $\lambda$. The density is $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. Over $n$ gaps the average gap is $m$ minutes.
items.question: Maximise $\ell(\lambda) = n\ln\lambda - \lambda n m$. Enter $\hat\lambda$ in terms of $m$.

feedback.correct: $\ell'(\lambda) = n/\lambda - nm = 0$ gives $\hat\lambda = 1/m$.
feedback.generic: Differentiate $\ell$ in $\lambda$, set it to 0, and solve.

byKey.mean: You gave the average gap. The rate is trades per minute, the reciprocal of minutes per trade.
byKey.square: Check the derivative of $n\ln\lambda$. It is $n/\lambda$, so $\lambda$ appears once.

explain.text: $\ell'(\lambda) = n/\lambda - nm$ is positive below $1/m$ and negative above, so $1/m$ is the maximum. A 4-minute average gap gives $\hat\lambda = 0.25$ trades a minute.

items.title: A test that usually misses
items.prose: A strategy truly earns 0.06% a day, with daily sd 1.2%. You test $H_0: \mu = 0$ one-sided at 5% on 400 days. The cut-off is 1.645. You are told $\Phi(0.645) = 0.7405$.
items.question: What is the power of the test? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Under $H_1$, $z$ is centred at $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$. Power is the chance it lands above 1.645.

byKey.beta: You gave $\beta$, the chance of missing the edge. Power is $1 - \beta$.
byKey.alpha: 5% is the chance of passing a strategy with no edge. Power is about a real edge.

explain.text: $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma = 0.06 \times 20/1.2 = 1$, so $z$ is centred at 1. It clears 1.645 with chance $\Phi(-0.645) = 0.2595$. A real edge fails this test about three times in four.

items.title: Two broken regressions
items.prose: Two regressions, two residual plots. Fit A: execution cost on order size, residuals against size. Fit B: a daily signal regression, residuals in time order, with Durbin-Watson $d = 0.34$.

state.caption: Fit A: residuals against order size

items.question: HC1 robust errors fix one of these problems but not the other. Tap the plot HC1 cannot fix.

feedback.correct: Fit B: long runs above and below zero, and $d$ far below 2. That needs HAC errors.
feedback.generic: HC1 lets each residual have its own variance. Which plot breaks independence instead?

byKey.left: Fit A's funnel is changing variance, which HC1 is built for. Fit B's slow waves are autocorrelation, and HC1 assumes independent days.

explain.text: Fit A's spread grows with size: changing variance, which HC1 handles. Fit B's residuals each resemble the day before, so $d \approx 2(1 - \hat\rho)$ is near 0. Only HAC errors allow for that; the naive $t$ is too big.

items.title: Draw the interval
items.prose: A fund's 64 monthly returns have mean 0.9% and sample sd 2.4%. The dot marks the mean.
items.question: Drag L and U to the ends of the 95% confidence interval for the true monthly mean, in %.

feedback.generic: The standard error is $2.4/\sqrt{64} = 0.3$. Go 1.96 of them either side of 0.9.

byKey.one-se: You went one standard error below the mean. 95% needs 1.96 of them.
byKey.one-se-up: You went one standard error above the mean. 95% needs 1.96 of them.
byKey.L: L is off. The lower end is $0.9 - 1.96 \times 0.3 = 0.31$.
byKey.U: U is off. The upper end is $0.9 + 1.96 \times 0.3 = 1.49$.

explain.text: The standard error is $2.4/\sqrt{64} = 0.3$, so the interval is $0.9 \pm 0.59$. It runs from 0.31% to 1.49% and excludes 0. The sd of 2.4% describes single months; the interval describes the mean.

items.title: Reading a backtest's p
items.prose: A backtest of a new signal reports $p = 0.02$ for $H_0$: the signal has no edge.
items.question: Which statements are right? Select all that apply.

options.text: With no edge, a backtest at least this good would turn up about 2% of the time.
A test at the 1% level would not reject $H_0$.
If this was the best of 40 variants tried, 0.02 overstates the evidence.
There is a 2% chance the signal has no edge.
options.why: You turned the conditional round. $p$ assumes no edge; it is not the chance of no edge.

options.text: There is a 98% chance the signal will make money live.
options.why: You read $1 - p$ as a chance of success. $p$ says nothing direct about the chance $H_1$ is true.

options.text: The edge must be large.
options.why: You read a small $p$ as a big effect. A tiny edge over a long backtest also gives a small $p$.

feedback.correct: A chance about the data under no edge, compared with your level, and weakened by searching.
feedback.generic: $p$ is $P(\text{a result this extreme} \mid H_0)$. Check each statement against that.

explain.text: $p = 0.02$ is a tail chance computed as if $H_0$ were true. It beats 5% but not 1%. Picked as the best of 40, a 0.02 is close to what noise alone produces.

items.title: Two momentum signals
items.prose: A model regresses next month's stock returns on 6-month and 12-month momentum. The two signals have correlation 0.8.
items.question: By what factor does this overlap multiply each slope's standard error, compared with uncorrelated signals? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\mathrm{VIF} = 1/(1 - 0.64) = 2.78$. The error grows by $\sqrt{2.78} = 1.67$.
feedback.generic: With two predictors, $R_j^2 = r^2$. The VIF scales the variance; the standard error scales by its root.

byKey.vif: 2.78 is the VIF, the factor on the variance. The standard error grows by its square root.
byKey.one-minus-r: You used $1/(1 - r)$. The VIF uses $R_j^2 = r^2 = 0.64$.
byKey.root-r: You took the root of $1/(1 - r)$. Put $r^2 = 0.64$ into the VIF first.

explain.text: Regressing one signal on the other gives $R_j^2 = 0.64$. So $\mathrm{VIF} = 2.78$ and each standard error is 1.67 times larger. Each slope's $t$ shrinks by that factor, even if the pair matters jointly.

items.title: A sceptical desk
items.prose: A desk gives a new trader a $\mathrm{Beta}(12, 8)$ prior for their hit rate: centred on 60%, worth 20 trades. The trader then wins 18 of 40 trades.
items.question: What is the posterior mean hit rate?

feedback.correct: The posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(30, 30)$, with mean $30/60 = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Add wins to $a$ and losses to $b$. The mean of $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ is $a/(a + b)$.

byKey.mle: 0.45 is the data alone, the maximum likelihood estimate. The prior still counts for 20 trades.
byKey.prior: 0.6 is the prior mean. The 40 trades should move it.
byKey.halfway: You averaged the prior mean and the MLE equally. The weights are 20 and 40 trades.

explain.text: $\mathrm{Beta}(12 + 18, 8 + 22) = \mathrm{Beta}(30, 30)$, with mean 0.5. That is $\tfrac{20}{60} \times 0.6 + \tfrac{40}{60} \times 0.45$. Each source is weighted by the trades it is worth.

items.title: Two strategies compared
items.prose: Strategy A ran 250 days: mean 0.08% a day, sd 1.0%. Strategy B ran 200 other days: mean $-0.02$%, sd 1.5%. Test whether their true means differ.
items.question: What is Welch's $t$ for A minus B? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: $t = (\bar x_A - \bar x_B)/\sqrt{s_A^2/n_A + s_B^2/n_B}$.

byKey.sum-se: You added the two standard errors. Variances add, so add the squares, then take the root.
byKey.sd-not-se: You divided by the sds without $\sqrt n$. Each mean's error uses $s^2/n$.

explain.text: The gap is 0.10% a day, and its standard error is 0.1235. So $t = 0.81$: no evidence that A beats B. A gap of a tenth of a percent is small beside daily sds of 1% to 1.5%.

items.title: Overlapping windows
items.prose: A backtest regresses each month's next-12-month return on a valuation signal. It uses 30 years of month-ends: 360 overlapping windows. The summary shows $t = 3.4$ and Durbin-Watson $d = 0.15$.
items.question: What is the honest next step?

options.text: Refit with HAC errors allowing at least 11 lags, as neighbouring windows share 11 months.
Refit with HC1 robust errors.
options.why: You reached for the fix for changing variance. HC1 still treats the 360 windows as independent.

options.text: Accept it: $t = 3.4$ clears even the stricter bar of 3.
options.why: You trusted a $t$ built on independent errors. Overlapping windows are near copies, so that $t$ is far too big.

options.text: Sample windows daily instead, for about 7,500 observations.
options.why: You added more overlap. Daily windows share 251 of 252 days, so they add almost no information.

feedback.correct: $d$ near 0 confirms the autocorrelation the overlap built in.
feedback.generic: What does $d = 0.15$ say about neighbouring residuals, and which errors allow for it?

explain.text: Each window shares 11 of its 12 months with the next, and $d \approx 2(1 - \hat\rho)$ gives $\hat\rho \approx 0.93$. Usual and HC1 errors assume independence, so they come out too small. HAC errors with 11 or more lags, or 30 non-overlapping years, give an honest $t$.

items.title: Bootstrapping a Sharpe ratio
items.prose: You want a 95% bootstrap interval for a strategy's Sharpe ratio. It has 500 daily returns, and you will use $B = 2{,}000$ resamples.
items.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Fix the random seed, so the interval can be reproduced
Draw 500 returns from the 500, with replacement
Compute the Sharpe ratio of that resample
Repeat the draw and the Sharpe ratio until you have 2,000 values
Report the 51st and the 1,950th values as the interval

feedback.correct: Seed, resample, recompute, repeat, sort, then drop 50 values from each end.
feedback.generic: Each resample needs its own statistic. The ends are read only after sorting all of them.

explain.text: $k = 0.025 \times 2{,}000 = 50$ values go from each end, leaving ranks 51 to 1,950. Drawing with replacement makes each resample differ from the data. Resampling single days assumes independent days; autocorrelated returns need blocks.

items.title: Ten signals, one screen
items.prose: Ten candidate signals were each backtested once. Their p-values are below. You control the false discovery rate with Benjamini-Hochberg at $q = 0.05$.
items.question: Tap every signal BH rejects.

feedback.correct: Reversal, Mom-12m, Low vol, Quality and Sentiment: ranks 1 to 5.
feedback.generic: Sort the p-values. Rank $k$ has the bar $k \times 0.05/10$. Find the largest rank under its bar.

byKey.stop-early: You stopped at the first rank that missed its bar. BH takes the largest rank that passes, and rank 5 does.
byKey.naive: You kept every $p$ below 0.05. Value, at rank 6, needs $p \le 6 \times 0.005 = 0.030$.
byKey.bonferroni: You used Bonferroni's flat bar of 0.005. BH's bar rises with rank: $k \times 0.005$.
byKey.r2: Value has $p = 0.041$ at rank 6, above its bar of 0.030.
byKey.r8: Seasonal's 0.090 at rank 7 is above its bar of 0.035.
byKey.r0: Mom-3m's 0.200 at rank 8 is far above its bar of 0.040.
byKey.r6: Size's 0.450 is far above every bar.
byKey.r4: Carry's 0.700 is the largest p-value of all.
byKey.r3: Quality misses its own bar, 0.021 against 0.020. It still goes, because rank 5 passes.
byKey.r9: Sentiment, at rank 5, has $0.024 \le 0.025$. It passes its bar.
byKey.r5: Low vol, at rank 3, has $0.012 \le 0.015$. It passes.
byKey.r1: Mom-12m, at rank 2, has $0.003 \le 0.010$. It passes.
byKey.r7: Reversal has the smallest p-value, 0.001, under its bar of 0.005.

explain.text: Sorted, the bars are $k \times 0.005$: 0.005, 0.010, up to 0.050. Rank 4 (0.021) misses 0.020, but rank 5 (0.024) clears 0.025. BH rejects every rank up to the largest that passes: five signals.

items.title: How long to prove alpha
items.prose: A fund earns a true alpha of 2% a year, with residual sd (tracking error) 6% a year. Monthly residuals are independent. Use $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) \approx s/\sqrt n$ on monthly data.
items.question: How many years of monthly returns until the alpha's expected $t$ statistic reaches 2?

feedback.correct: Monthly alpha 0.167% and monthly $s = 6/\sqrt{12} = 1.73\%$. $t = 2$ needs 432 months: 36 years.
feedback.generic: Convert to months: the mean divides by 12, the sd by $\sqrt{12}$. Then solve $0.167\sqrt n/1.73 = 2$.

byKey.sd-by-12: You divided the sd by 12. Volatility scales with the root of time, so divide by $\sqrt{12}$.
byKey.months: 432 is the number of months. The question asks for years.

explain.text: The alpha's $t$ is the information ratio times root years: $(2/6)\sqrt T = 2$ gives $T = 36$. A genuinely good manager needs decades to prove it. So a short record is weak evidence either way.

items.title: Volatility by maximum likelihood
items.prose: A stock's 21 daily returns have mean 0.2% and $\sum r_i^2 = 42.84$ (%²). Model them as independent normal.
items.question: What is the maximum likelihood estimate of the annualised volatility, in %? Use 252 trading days.

feedback.correct: $\sum (r_i - \bar r)^2 = 42.84 - 21 \times 0.04 = 42$. So $\hat\sigma = \sqrt 2 = 1.414\%$ a day, 22.45% a year.
feedback.generic: Centre first: $\sum (r_i - \bar r)^2 = \sum r_i^2 - n\bar r^2$. The MLE divides by $n$; then scale by $\sqrt{252}$.

byKey.n-1: You divided by $n - 1 = 20$. That gives the unbiased $s^2$; the MLE divides by $n$.
byKey.no-centre: You skipped the mean. Subtract $n\bar r^2 = 0.84$ before dividing.
byKey.times-252: You multiplied the sd by 252. Variance scales with time, so the sd scales with $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.variance: You annualised the variance, $2 \times 252$, and stopped. Take its square root.

explain.text: Setting $\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2 = 0$ gives $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1n\sum (r_i - \bar r)^2 = 42/21 = 2$. The daily sd is 1.414%, and $1.414\sqrt{252} = 22.45\%$. On the variance the MLE is biased low by $(n - 1)/n$.

items.title: A Sharpe ratio, tested and deflated
items.prose: A due-diligence tool takes a fund's monthly returns, in %, and the number of strategies tried, $N$. It reports four numbers: the annualised Sharpe ratio, its $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T$ with $T$ in years, the one-sided p-value, and the Bonferroni p-value $\min(1, Np)$.
items.question: Complete `sharpe_report` so it returns the four numbers, each rounded to 6 places.

    return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(z / math.sqrt(2)))

def sharpe_report(monthly, n_tried):
    n = len(monthly)
    mean = sum(monthly) / n
    sd = ...       # sample sd, dividing by n - 1
    sharpe = ...   # annualised Sharpe ratio
    t = ...        # Sharpe times root of years
    p = ...        # one-sided p-value, H1: mean > 0

widget.solution:
import math

def phi(z):
    # standard normal cdf
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(z / math.sqrt(2)))

def sharpe_report(monthly, n_tried):
    n = len(monthly)
    mean = sum(monthly) / n
    ss = sum((r - mean) ** 2 for r in monthly)
    sd = math.sqrt(ss / (n - 1))
    sharpe = mean / sd * math.sqrt(12)
    t = sharpe * math.sqrt(n / 12)
    p = 1 - phi(t)
    p_adj = min(1.0, n_tried * p)
    out = (sharpe, t, p, p_adj)
    return [round(v, 6) for v in out]
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each list is rounded to 6 places and compared with math.isclose. numpy is available but loads slowly; pure Python with `math.erf` is enough here.

feedback.correct: Sharpe from the monthly mean and sd, $t$ from the record's length, then the tail and its Bonferroni penalty.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. For `[4, -2] * 18` the mean is 1 and $s = 3.042$, so the Sharpe ratio is 1.139.

byKey.test-1: The 36-month fund is off. Check the sd divides by $n - 1$, the $\sqrt{12}$, and that $p$ is one-sided.
byKey.test-2: With 12 strategies tried, the Bonferroni p-value is 12 times the one-sided p-value.
byKey.test-4: A losing fund has $p$ above 0.5. Bonferroni then caps $Np$ at 1.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with its formula.

explain.text:
The Sharpe ratio's $t$ equals the mean over its standard error, $\bar r/(s/\sqrt n)$. Searching $N$ strategies multiplies the chance of a lucky one, so Bonferroni multiplies $p$ by $N$.

```python
ss = sum((r - mean) ** 2 for r in monthly)
sd = math.sqrt(ss / (n - 1))
sharpe = mean / sd * math.sqrt(12)
t = sharpe * math.sqrt(n / 12)
p = 1 - phi(t)
p_adj = min(1.0, n_tried * p)
```

items.title: A factor regression by hand
items.prose: A risk system must report a fund's factor regression without statsmodels. `cols` is a list of factor return columns. Fit $\mathbf{y}$ on a constant and the columns by the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$.
items.question: Complete `factor_report` so it returns the coefficients, their $t$ statistics and the adjusted $R^2$, each rounded to 6 places.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def factor_report(y, cols):
    y = np.array(y, dtype=float)
    n, k = len(y), len(cols)
    cols = [np.array(c, dtype=float) for c in cols]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n)] + cols)
    coef = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
    e = y - X @ coef
    s2 = (e @ e) / (n - k - 1)
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.diag(np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
    t = coef / se
    r2 = 1 - (e @ e) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
    r2_adj = 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1)
    out = [*coef, *t, r2_adj]
    return [round(float(v), 6) for v in out]

`np.linalg.solve` finds $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ without forming an inverse for the fit. Each $t$ is a coefficient over its standard error, the root of a diagonal entry of $s^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$. Dividing SSE by $n - k - 1$ is what makes the errors match statsmodels.

items.title: How many trades to see an edge
items.prose: A signal claims a 53% hit rate. You will test $H_0: p = 0.5$ one-sided at 5%, and want 80% power if the claim is true. Under $H_0$ one trade has sd 0.5. Use $z_{0.05} = 1.645$ and $z_{0.20} = 0.842$.
items.question: How many trades do you need? Round up to a whole trade.

feedback.generic: Use $n = \left((z_\alpha + z_\beta)\,\sigma/\delta\right)^2$ with $\delta = 0.53 - 0.5 = 0.03$.

byKey.no-power: You set $z_\beta = 0$, which gives only 50% power. Add 0.842 for 80%.
byKey.no-square: You stopped at $\sqrt n = 41.45$. Square it.
byKey.two-sided: You used 1.96, the two-sided cut-off. This test is one-sided.
byKey.level: You used 0.53 as $\delta$. The edge is the gap from the null, $0.53 - 0.5$.

explain.text: The hit rate's standard error is $0.5/\sqrt n$. For 80% power the true 0.53 must sit $1.645 + 0.842$ standard errors above 0.5. So $\sqrt n = 41.45$ and $n = 1{,}719$: a small edge needs a long record.

items.title: Judging a track record
items.prompt:
A manager pitches her fund to your investment committee. Over 36 months its returns averaged 1.0% a month, with sample sd 3.0%. A regression on the market gives a monthly alpha of 0.6%, standard error 0.4%, and a beta of 0.9. Late in the meeting she mentions it was the best of 12 strategies her firm ran over that period.

(a) Find the annualised Sharpe ratio and its $t$ statistic. Give the one-sided p-value.

(b) Find the alpha's $t$ statistic and an approximate 95% interval for the monthly alpha. Say what each means.

(c) Allow for the 12 strategies. The one-sided Bonferroni bar is $z_{1 - 0.05/12} = 2.64$.

(d) If the Sharpe ratio held, how long a record would clear that bar?

(e) Say what you would ask for before investing, and why.

You may use $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$ and the 5% two-sided $t$ cut-off of 2.03 for 34 degrees of freedom.

rubric.text: Finds the annualised Sharpe ratio 1.15, $t = 2.0$ and one-sided $p \approx 0.023$.
Finds $t_\alpha = 1.5$ and an interval of about $-0.2\%$ to $1.4\%$, and says it includes 0 without proving no skill.
Adjusts for 12 strategies: Bonferroni $p \approx 0.27$ or $t$ below 2.64, concluding the evidence does not survive.
Asks for at least three things with reasons, including the other strategies' records and an out-of-sample record.

explain.text: The Sharpe ratio's $t$ is 2.0 alone, but the best of 12 needs 2.64. The alpha's interval includes zero. Ask for the whole search and a live record before believing it.
